meta.title: Division 296 and the prudential framework
meta.subtitle: What the new tax on large superannuation balances asks of us — and what it does not

bottom_line: This is not a proposal. Division 296 has been law since March and started on 1 July 2026. We are already inside the first measurement year. The final regulations were registered twelve days before it began, and the Tax Office guidance explaining how to do the calculation is still unwritten.

It is not a liquidity event, and we should say so. In our own System Risk Stress Test, six large funds absorbed $174 billion of cumulative liquidity demand — just under 16 per cent of net assets — while largely avoiding sales of unlisted assets, primarily selling listed equities instead. Division 296 outflows are a small fraction of that. Leading with a liquidity warning would be wrong, and people in the room will know it.

The real change is that a trustee judgement now feeds an individual member's personal tax bill. Every large fund we supervise must split fund earnings between members on a 'fair and reasonable' basis it designs itself, and report that figure to the Tax Office. Two funds holding identical assets for identical members can lawfully report different numbers. No standard governs how that judgement is made, signed off or independently checked.

The framework mostly already covers this. Of 23 instruments we examined, 11 need no change at all and only one needs amending — our own reporting standard, which cannot see above $1 million. What is missing is guidance, supervisory attention, and a seat in the room where the rules are actually being written.

why_prudential.text: The tax is assessed on the member, but the work lands on the trustee. Funds must now calculate the tax base themselves and attribute a share to each affected member — a function that did not exist before, and that no prudential standard was written for.

The attribution standard is a discretion, not a formula. Funds with more than six members apply a 'fair and reasonable' test of their own design; funds with six or fewer get a prescribed formula and a compulsory actuarial certificate. That boundary is fund size, not who regulates — small APRA funds sit on the prescribed side despite being ours. The effect is that the loose standard lands on the large funds holding almost all the money.

This is a member-equity problem wearing a tax label. A fund produces one annual whole-of-fund tax figure; a member's entitlement is a daily unit price built on a different basis. The two cannot be reconciled exactly, so any method is an estimate that advantages some members over others.

Industry has asked for the judgement to be put beyond challenge — that trustees' attribution decisions sit outside AFCA's jurisdiction and that funds not handle member disputes about them at all. Either outcome creates a problem: a new class of complaint, or members with no recourse against a judgement that sets their personal tax.

We cannot see the affected population. Our highest published balance bracket is $1 million and above — one third of the lower threshold. And because the threshold is measured across everything a person holds, including self-managed funds, no per-fund collection could ever produce that view.

framework_intro: The most useful finding here is a negative one. Division 296 does not require us to rewrite the prudential framework. We examined 23 instruments: 11 need no change at all, 7 need only supervisory attention, 4 warrant updated guidance, and exactly one needs amending — SRS 611.0, our own member accounts collection, whose highest balance bracket stops at a third of the lower threshold. The authority is already there. SPG 530 expressly names a change in government policy affecting access to member assets as a liquidity stress factor. CPS 230 already forces fund administration to be treated as a critical operation. Boards already sign an annual risk declaration. What is missing is not power — it is guidance telling trustees these obligations bite on a tax event, supervision aimed at the cohort least able to cope, and data that would let us see any of it.

recommendations.text: Confirm our engagement, then secure a prudential seat. The remaining design work has moved into a non-public ATO co-design group of the Tax Office, large funds, administrators and one industry body, and both public consultations have closed. We could find no record of APRA participation or any published APRA material on this measure — but that is a search result, not an internal audit, so confirm it before it is said out loud. If it holds, ask to participate or observe and put our position on attribution in writing.

Write to RSE licensees. A short letter stating that existing obligations already apply to Division 296 readiness — fund administration as a critical operation under CPS 230, policy-driven liquidity stress under SPG 530, and the annual board risk declaration under SPS 220 — costs us nothing, needs no new instrument, and sets an expectation before the first measurement year closes. We have published nothing on this measure to date.
Form a view on whether the attribution judgement should be reviewable, and say so. This is a member-outcomes question, not a tax question, and it is being decided without us.

Target the cohort we have already named. Our December 2024 thematic review found 12 of 23 large trustees needed material improvement in valuation or liquidity governance, and in June 2026 we took enforcement action against five platform trustees. Those same platform and wrap trustees hold the highest share of very large accounts and face the hardest attribution problem. This is an evidence-based shortlist that needs no new data.

Require funds to model the 30 June 2027 window. In the first year only, liability turns solely on the balance at that date, making it a publicly known, one-off incentive to withdraw or restructure — landing in the sector's busiest operational period. SPG 530 already lets us require this stress to be modelled.

Fix our own blind spot. Amend the SRS 611.0 balance brackets so they extend above the thresholds, and decompose the SRS 551.0 liquidity collection by driver so Division 296 outflows are not lost inside a single net figure. Accept that neither gives us total superannuation balance — only the ATO holds that — so agree an information-sharing arrangement.

redteam_intro: The draft register was attacked by three independent adversarial reviewers before it reached this page: a hostile fact-checker instructed to refute rather than agree, a grading sceptic instructed to hunt for inflated ratings, and a completeness critic instructed to find what had been left out. perimeter.title: Most of the affected population is outside our perimeter
perimeter.subtitle: Treasury expected 31,800 of about 80,000 affected individuals to sit in APRA-regulated funds or exempt public sector schemes
perimeter.note: Source: Treasury Impact Analysis. Self-managed funds are regulated by the ATO, not by us — so roughly six in ten affected members sit where we have no standards, no data and no supervisory reach.
